'''James Arthur Birchler''' is an American biologist who is currently Curators' Distinguished Professor at [[University of Missouri]] where he studies gene dosage, polyploidy, and cytogenetics in both [[maize]] and [[Drosophila melanogaster|drosophila]]. In 2002 he was named a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref name="James Birchler">{{Cite web |url=https://www.aaas.org/fellow/birchler-james |title=James Birchler |publisher=aaas.org |accessdate=May 13, 2017 |archive-date=August 29, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180829072933/https://www.aaas.org/fellow/birchler-james |url-status=dead }}</ref>  and in 2011 he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/james-a-birchler-qsyoyb/|title=James Birchler|website=www.nasonline.org|access-date=2018-08-29}}</ref><ref name="PNAS Profile" /> In 2017 he was named the SEC Professor of the Year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thesecu.com/news/missouris-james-birchler-named-2017-sec-professor-of-the-year/|title=Missouri's James Birchler Named 2017 SEC Professor of the Year {{!}} SECU|website=www.thesecu.com|language=en-US|access-date=2018-08-29}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Birchler was born on a farm near [[Red Bud, Illinois]]. He attended Eastern Illinois University where he initially majored in education and was mentored by ethnobotanist Charles Arzeni. After completing his degree at EIU in 1972, ultimately majoring in biology with a minor in zoology, he moved to Indiana University Bloomington where he studied maize dosage effects using [[B chromosome]]s with Drew Schwartz, graduating in 1977.<ref name="PlantCellProfile">{{Cite journal|url= |doi=10.1105/tpc.19.00489|title=James A. Birchler|year=2019|last1=Frank|first1=Margaret|last2=Harkess|first2=Alex|last3=Washburn|first3=Jacob|journal=The Plant Cell|volume=31|issue=10|pages=2277–2280|pmid=31266846|pmc=6790089|bibcode=2019PlanC..31.2277F }}</ref> Between 1978 and 1985 he worked as a postdoc studying gene dosage mechanisms in fruit flies, first at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] with Ed Grell, and then at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] with [[Kenneth Paigen]]. In 1985 he was hired as an assistant professor at Harvard University, and in 1991 he moved to the University of Missouri.<ref name="PNAS Profile" />

==Research==
Birchler is known for his contributions to the study of gene dosage, dosage compensation, and gene balance using both [[maize]] (''Zea mays'') and fruit flies ([[Drosophila melanogaster]]) as model organisms.<ref name=":0" /> He is also known for his lab's contributions to maize [[Karyotype|karyotyping]] by "[[chromosome painting]]" or [[fluorescence in situ hybridization]]. Birchler and his lab have also leveraged this tool and maize B-A [[chromosomal translocation]]s to study the function and inactivation of [[centromere]]s. Birchler's lab also developed the first engineered [[minichromosome]]s in plants, by using [[telomere]] repeat sequences to truncate [[B chromosome]]s in [[maize]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yu|first1=Weichang|last2=Yau|first2=Yuan-Yeu|last3=Birchler|first3=James A.|date=2015-09-15|title=Plant artificial chromosome technology and its potential application in genetic engineering|journal=Plant Biotechnology Journal|language=en|volume=14|issue=5|pages=1175–1182|doi=10.1111/pbi.12466|pmid=26369910|issn=1467-7644|doi-access=free|pmc=11389009}}</ref> James A. Birchler also developed Fast-Flowering Mini-Maize<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McCaw|first1=Morgan E.|last2=Wallace|first2=Jason G.|last3=Albert|first3=Patrice S.|last4=Buckler|first4=Edward S.|last5=Birchler|first5=James A.|date=2016-01-01|title=Fast-Flowering Mini-Maize: Seed to Seed in 60 Days|url=http://www.genetics.org/content/early/2016/07/15/genetics.116.191726|journal=Genetics|volume=204|issue=1|language=en|pages=35–42|doi=10.1534/genetics.116.191726|issn=0016-6731|pmid=27440866|pmc=5012399}}</ref> as a small, rapid-cycling model for maize.
